# 2.14.0

The lazy store line no longer wedges when a subscriber owes more than one read window.

- **An interrupted catch-up used to make no progress at all.** `read()` walked in two halves —
  keys at or before the cursor that changed (what the subscriber missed), then keys past it
  (never delivered) — and only the second half advanced `cursor.key`, while `cursor.revision`
  advanced only once the first half completed. So when the catch-up alone spent the byte budget,
  neither field moved and the returned cursor was identical to the one passed in. Every later
  read redid the same work: the subscriber received the same alphabetical prefix forever and the
  rest of its mirror stayed stale.

  This is not only a reconnect hazard. A healthy live subscriber has its cursor at the last key,
  so its whole key range is catch-up region; one burst of changes larger than `readBytes` between
  two polls wedged it just the same. The reason it went unreported is an accidental rescue:
  pruning a tombstone advances `oldestProvableRevision`, and a wedged cursor whose revision falls
  below it is refused as `stale` and restarts from scratch. On a line that deletes keys the wedge
  therefore self-heals within `tombstoneKeepMs` — expensively, and invisibly. On a line that
  never deletes, it does not heal.

- **The cursor is now a two-piece revision floor, and the walk is one pass.** A key is sent when
  its revision is newer than the floor the cursor claims for it: `catchUp.revision` at or before
  `catchUp.key`, `cursor.revision` at or before `cursor.key`, and everything past `cursor.key`
  has never been delivered. Catch-up and fill were never two algorithms, only two arms of that
  one rule, so a truncated read now records where it stopped and the next one continues instead
  of restarting. Tombstones join the same ordered walk rather than being iterated in `Map` order
  beside it, which is what made a resume position expressible at all.

  Two claims are always enough: a resumed catch-up walks its region from the start, so the
  boundary never splits into a third step. When live churn pulls the walk back to an earlier key,
  the boundary is lowered unconditionally — lowering a floor only costs a re-send, whereas
  refusing to lower it would leave those changes unrecorded and reopen the same loop one region
  deeper.

- **Public surface: `StoreLazyCursor` gains an optional `catchUp: {key, revision}`.** Additive and
  backward compatible — a persisted cursor without it reads as "catch-up complete", which is
  exactly what it claimed. Subscribers treat the cursor as opaque and round-trip it, so no caller
  changes. The one direction that is not compatible is a NEW cursor replayed against an OLD host,
  which silently drops the unreconciled remainder; that requires an explicit `lineId` deliberately
  carried across deployments, since the default per-instance id makes such a cursor stale anyway.

- **`filled` now requires the catch-up to be complete**, not just the fill frontier to be at the
  end of the key space. It previously reported a converged mirror while the read that produced it
  had been truncated. Downstream this only tightens guarantees: `syncStoreLazyLine().filled`
  resolves at real convergence, `fillOnly` no longer closes with an outstanding remainder, and the
  poll interval stays at `fillIntervalMs` until the backlog drains instead of throttling it.

Proof, not assertion: `oracle/regression/lazy-line-livelock.spec.ts` fails against the previous
code with "the cursor never moved across 48 reads" — 48 being four times the number needed to
carry the whole backlog, so the failure is a livelock and not a slow line. Its second
case is a control that passed before and still passes — a deletion catch-up already converged,
because a tombstone costs `key.length + 4` bytes and drains long before the budget — and it is
pinned so the reordered walk cannot lose that. The existing `observe/store-lazy-line.test.ts`
(21 checks, including "the consumer budget bounds every read" and "mirror converges while the
store keeps changing") passes unchanged.
